But even as Trump offers an opening for China to pose as the status quo power within the US–China dyad, Beijing faces tensions between its ambitions to project itself as a responsible leader and the imperatives of the geopolitical competition it faces.

In this week’s lead article, Kerry Brown reviews the outcomes of the recent Two Sessions of the National People’s Congress and the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Congress, which although broadly demure in their outputs nonetheless highlighted how the Chinese elites see steeling the economy for a prolonged period of an economic cold war — and maybe an actual war — as a primary national goal. ‘With the United States retreating into isolationism’, Brown writes, the leadership feels that ‘China is being pushed into action’, with ‘the accelerated weaning off US and other foreign technology … now a national priority’.

not only with industrialised economies, but also with developing countries who are faced with the redirection of Chinese capacity away from markets from which it is being excluded.

China is promising moves to boost domestic demand through measures that will lift consumer spending, though to what effect remains to be seen. If Xi can pull off an actual rebalance between the international and domestic impetus to growth, it would remove a potential bugbear in relations with strategically crucial governments in Southeast Asia, who are themselves flirting with protectionism ostensibly to shield local industries from an onslaught of Chinese manufactured goods that are less welcome in the US market as Mari Pangestu and Shiro Armstrong have recently pointed out in East Asia Forum.

China now appears more invested in maintaining a version of the status quo that allows it to pursue its own agenda within the existing international institutional framework — freed up to do so by the United States’ new spoiler role.

But it is a role that has been won by default, not by taking leadership in supplying regional and global public goods — let alone collaborating with partners, such as the United States did in the years after World War 2, to actually wrap itself in multilaterally-negotiated rules. BRICS is no Bretton Woods, to put it mildly.
